Avoid using combinator chains in ways that hurt readability. Specifically:
Avoid long and complex combinator chains.

Don’t construct combinator chains in the header of a for loop. Instead,
assign the combinator chain to a variable, then consume that variable in the
for loop.

Avoid Iterator::for_each unless you’re convinced you have a good reason. A
for loop is usually easier to read.

Combinators are preferable for shorter chains and for cases where the
combinator itself provides a lot of logic that would otherwise have to be
written out in the corresponding for loop.
Examples
Complex combinator chains

Here’s an example of a combinator chain that is hard to read because it involves
conditionals and mutates external state:
The corresponding for loop is easier to read:
Combinator chains in for loops
Avoid constructing a combinator chain in the header of a for loop:

Instead, assign the combinator chain to a variable. This reduces clutter, and
the variable name documents what the combinator chain does:
When to prefer a combinator chain
Here’s an example where a combinator chain is preferable:
let threshold_exceeded = values.iter().any(|&v| v > threshold);

The corresponding for loop is harder to read and reinvents the logic contained
in any():
Don’t call panic::catch_unwind
Use of panic::catch_unwind is prohibited in first-party Rust code.
Exceptions:

It is acceptable as a defense in depth mechanism as long as it is never
relied upon for any properties. A codebase that is already attempting to
avoid panics may choose to wrap critical entry points with a catch_unwind
recovery mechanism just in case a panic slips through. Code authors must
convince the reviewer that the codebase is doing most of what it can to
avoid panics. This exception only applies to code that has the possibility
of being run with panic=unwind (so this does not apply to
Chrome, Android,
Fuchsia).
Rationale

Rust code may be used in many environments, and panic::catch_unwind will only
function correctly in environments with panic=unwind. While the final panic
disposition of prod binaries has not yet been determined, Chrome, Android, and
Fuchsia all require panic=abort.
Prefer format! / write! for concatenation and substitution

Prefer format!() and write!() to other alternatives in the following
situations:

To concatenate more than two strings. For example, use
format!("{a}{b}{c}") instead of a + b + c.

To perform substitutions on a literal string (instead of using
str::replace).
Rationale

format! / write! require fewer allocations than concatenating strings
using +.
Prefer standard format strings to inventing your own templating syntax.
Use the right per-codebase test framework
Most codebases use their own specific test framework rather than #[test].

items.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
items.author: alphax314
items.summary: TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model
items.text:
TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type pythoon to see that it's not a real shell.

The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly.

When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs.

Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal.

A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what ls or cat should print.

What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output.

The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker.
Jump to example videos

How it sees a terminal

Standard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like esc in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: clear wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen.

I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell. The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it.

A session

Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is.

The size is part of the input, not fixed at 32×96. In the demo, you can set the rows and columns when creating a custom starting screen.

BOS SCREEN_START 32 96
ROW_0 0 'simedw@laptop:~$ '
CURSOR 0 17 1
SCREEN_END

This also lets me start partway through an application. Give it a bash prompt, vim buffer or a game of snake, and the model tries to continue from there. (It does better from bash.)

After that, each keypress goes in as the raw bytes a real terminal would send. Letters are themselves, Enter is \r, Escape is 0x1b and ← is ESC [ D and so on.

INPUT_START 'l' INPUT_END

The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor ends up:

OUTPUT_START
ROW_0 17 'l'
CURSOR 0 18 1
OUTPUT_END

In words: on row 0, starting at column 17, write l, then move the cursor to row 0, column 18. The last 1 means the cursor is visible, since full-screen apps sometimes hide it.

Nothing gets cleared first. New characters are simply drawn over the old ones.

I didn't need new tokens for characters. Qwen already has tokens for all 256 byte values, which I reuse for characters, coordinates and other small numbers. So a coordinate like 17 takes one token, not two.

Time is an input too. If nothing is pressed, the model gets a WAIT token with a duration instead of a key, which is how snake keeps moving on its own.

Copying rows

When you reach the bottom of the terminal window and press enter, every line has to move up by one. I could just ask the model to output every row again in its new place, but that's around 3,000 tokens for a single keypress.

So I added a COPY operation instead:

ROW_0 COPY 1
ROW_1 COPY 2
ROW_2 COPY 3
...

Each operation copies a row from the previous screen. In this example, the old row 1 becomes row 0, row 2 becomes row 1, and so on.

A scroll now costs three tokens per row instead of roughly 96.

The same trick covers clearing the screen, inserting and deleting lines in vim, and navigating man pages. You can also copy a row and then overwrite part of it.

Altogether, the model uses a tiny vocabulary of 333 tokens: 256 byte tokens, 64 row tokens and a handful of special operations. Decoding is grammar-constrained, so every prediction is a valid screen update.

That tiny vocabulary comes back later, when I squeeze the model into a browser.

Generating the training data

I initially looked for existing datasets of terminal recordings, including asciinema, but couldn't find one with the precise keystroke-to-screen alignment I needed.

Luckily it wasn't too hard to create my own.

The basic idea was to generate believable terminal sessions by running real commands inside Docker containers, recording every keypress and the screen after each one.

The synthetic recipe was:

Randomize usernames, hostnames, prompt styles, terminal sizes.

Randomize directories and files based on a fictional persona (developer, sysadmin, etc.).

Pick 6–24 weighted activities (modify files, vim, python, tmux, etc.).

Track state, so sessions mostly open files that exist.

Type like a person: one keypress at a time, with tab completion etc. I set the typo rate to 1.2%, which is generous to me.

35% of sessions start partway through, forcing the model to learn to work from any state.

The terminal size was mostly 32×96, with some 24×80 and 40×120, so the model doesn't overfit to one size.

I kept expanding the dataset as the model became more capable, and finally landed on 336k episodes, which corresponds to roughly 2B tokens. For comparison, the base model saw around 18T tokens during training.

Training

I used Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B as the starting point. I needed a small model to get close to realtime performance. Being a coding model, it had also already seen plenty of CLI usage.

I started off by doing straightforward supervised fine-tuning: give a screen history and a keypress, predict the screen delta produced by the real terminal.

Ordinary typing was learned quickly: a letter appears, backspace removes it, the cursor moves.

In longer sessions, though, errors started to compound: a mistake in a filename propagated through the rest of the session.

Learning from its own mistakes

To address this I took a page from DAgger, where a model learns from the states it visits rather than just the ideal demonstrations.

For each training example:

Pick a point in a recorded session, usually close to the command that produces the output.

Let the model predict the next 1-4 events.

Compare the resulting screen with the real recorded screen.

If the difference is small enough, construct a correction that repairs the model's screen on the next keypress.

Continue training on the corrected frame and a few subsequent real events.

The delta takes the model's incorrect screen to the correct next screen. In essence, it learns to "repair" its own mistakes.

There's one important restriction: the model must have enough information to infer the correction. Any words introduced by a correction must have appeared on an earlier real screen or in the user's typing, not just in the model's own predictions.

For example, if the model misspells a filename that appeared earlier, I can teach it to fix that. But if it lists a filename it has never seen, I can't expect it to get it right.

Training on those examples would actually reward hallucinations, which I really don't need more of.

About a third of the sampled sessions produced useful correction examples. I repeated this in three rounds, each time collecting mistakes from the latest model.

Self-correction was one of the more effective training changes. Along with some additional training data, it improved PresetBench (defined below) from 24/47 to 38/47 at int4.

In total, training the model and its later refinements took roughly 75 GPU-hours on an RTX 4090.

Testing

I use three tests. ShellBench has 106 commands across 24 handwritten bash sessions, scored by exact output. PresetBench has 47 scripted cases drawn from failures I hit in the demo. Neither test appears in the training data.

The memory test has 32 worlds. Each writes two random values to two files, then reads them back in separate sessions. A world passes only if both readbacks are exact, giving 64 readbacks overall. The names and values never appear in training.

How much does fine-tuning help?

Model

ShellBench /106

File readbacks /13

Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, prompted

52

2

Qwen3-0.6B, prompted

60

3

WorldTUI

80

9

The biggest difference was memory: WorldTUI got 9/13 readbacks right, compared with 2/13 and 3/13 for the prompted models.

It's still far from a reliable filesystem. It handles familiar commands fairly well, but combining them in new ways can quickly break things. For example, after echo green >> colors, running cat colors often doesn't show the appended line.

Making it fast

For a while I stayed away from autoregressive models altogether. A full redraw is around 3,000 tokens, and generating those one at a time seemed hopeless for something that's supposed to feel like a terminal.

But they just performed so much better than the alternatives I tried, so I gave in. With one token at a time, typing felt fine at ~38 ms per key, but anything that redraws the whole screen (vim test.txt, man, clear) took up to 12 s on my RTX 4090, exactly as feared. Plenty of time to reconsider whether I needed the manual. And I wanted this to run on my Mac, in near real-time.

Rows in parallel

What I'd missed was that most rows in a frame don't depend on each other, so there's no reason to generate them one after another. I run one batch element per row. Each gets the same previous history (including KV cache) but generates only its own update.

That changes the decoding cost from the sum of all rows, up to 3,000 steps, to the length of the longest row, roughly 100 steps.

The cursor then becomes its own step at the end that can see the whole set of row updates.

This required a matching attention mask during training, but the speed improvement was worth it. Large-frame p95 latency dropped from 6.7 s to 0.87 s.

Large-frame p95 latency (RTX 4090) ↓

Rows that can't talk to each other

This might sound too good to be true, and it was.
The issue is that since rows are independent, they can't coordinate, which led to vim opening on row 3 instead of row 0, or several rows adding food for snake at once.

The solution was speculative decoding.

Normally speculative decoding uses a small model to draft tokens and a larger model to verify them. Thanks to causal attention, several tokens can be verified in a single forward pass.

Here I use the same model for both: the parallel rows produce a draft, which the model then verifies sequentially.

The verifier keeps tokens up to the first disagreement. From there it generates its own correction and re-proposes the remaining draft.

In the browser on my M4 Mac, typing a single character takes about 60ms. A larger update like man test takes 2.5s sequentially, or 0.9s with parallel drafting and verification.

Making it smaller

I started with Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, which has roughly 494M parameters. I really wanted a web demo, so I needed to shrink it. The embedding table for its 151,936-token vocabulary is 136M parameters. I only need my 333 tokens, so I can drop almost all of it, which takes the model from 494M to about 360M parameters (990MB → 716MB).

I then quantized it to int4, which brought it to 208 MB.

The browser demo uses a custom JavaScript implementation of the Qwen decoder, with compute shaders written in WGSL and run through WebGPU. The shaders unpack the 4-bit weights during inference. Activations and the attention cache use 32-bit floats. All inference runs locally in the tab.

Distilling

Distilling it into fewer layers taught me something about which layers memory depends on. The teacher was an earlier checkpoint, which scored 78/106 on ShellBench. Removing just layer 7 without retraining barely changed next-token accuracy: 99.3% fell to 98.9%. But exact memory readbacks fell from 64/64 to 0/64. These tests fed in the true history, so the failure wasn't caused by errors compounding on the model's own output.

My first distilled student kept every even-numbered layer, but used the final layer, 23, instead of 22. It still wrote plausible terminal output, but returned the right value in only 31/64 memory readbacks. It always printed one of the two values it had written, but picked the wrong one about half the time. That's chance, and it hadn't recovered after 480M training tokens.

That student had dropped layers 1, 7, 15 and 22. A 16-layer student that kept those four passed all 32 memory test worlds, with 64/64 exact readbacks. It still passed all 32 worlds at 4-bit, at about 138MB. There was a cost elsewhere, though: it got 65 ShellBench commands right against the teacher's 78. So a student can look fine and have quietly lost its memory.

In the end I gave up on distilling it.

What it can do

Memory

This was the part I was most interested in.
Generating a convincing directory listing is easy. What I wanted was to create a file, edit it, wander off, and come back to find it unchanged.

The first time I started tmux, opened a file in vim, changed it, saved it and then in a different tmux window read the updated contents with cat, I felt like Dr. Frankenstein: it's alive!

Other applications

It was very important to me that this should work beyond the bash prompt, so I trained on vim, python, man pages, snake and even tmux.

In vim, it handles the mode switch on esc and lets me save, quit or go back into insert mode.

What really blew my mind was tmux: I can create multiple panes, do various things in each and jump between them. It's not perfect, but it's a small model.

It even manages environment variables and variable expansion.

Python

Since the base model is a coding model, I was curious how it would handle the Python REPL. It makes a decent attempt: small additions are usually right, and list comprehensions return a list, though often with the wrong contents. It's also slightly forgiving of typos: pythoon launches Python, but ython doesn't.

What doesn't work

I didn't allow the Docker containers internet access, so tools like lynx are fairly boring.
Python can handle very simple operations, but anything harder produces answers that remind me of GPT-3-era hallucinations.

Sometimes, when I create nested directories, it gets lost and all of a sudden I'm in a different path.
There's clearly a lot of room to improve consistency.

In my testing, the demo ran about 20× slower in Firefox than in Chrome. It uses WebGPU in both. I haven't managed to establish the cause.

As always with projects like this, I tried to solve it myself first and only then looked at how others had approached it.

Back in 2022, people were already prompting ChatGPT to act as a Linux terminal. More recently, GameNGen simulated Doom using diffusion, and NeuralOS tackled a desktop GUI.

WorldTUI is closer to the original ChatGPT terminal trick, except that it's trained specifically on keypresses and screen updates, including full-screen applications like vim and tmux.

Summary

I had a blast building this. Is it useful? Not really. But for a 360M-parameter model running in a browser tab, it's far better than I expected.

What interests me most is that it manages to maintain a somewhat consistent world without implementing any of the rules underneath.

It's obviously a pretty weak world model, and I'd love to see how far this approach could go with better consistency and a different way of generating screen updates, perhaps using diffusion instead of autoregressive decoding.

One experiment I want to try next is training on thousands of randomly generated applications, each with its own controls and rules. The idea is to see whether the model can learn to predict the behaviour of an application it has never encountered before, given enough contextual clues.

Try it here. It's a 208 MB download, runs entirely locally, and works best in Chrome. Try to break it, and let me know what you find.

I'll post the weights soon and add the download link here.

The delta takes the model's incorrect screen to the correct next screen. In essence, it learns to "repair" its own mistakes.

There's one important restriction: the model must have enough information to infer the correction. Any words introduced by a correction must have appeared on an earlier real screen or in the user's typing, not just in the model's own predictions.
For example, if the model misspells a filename that appeared earlier, I can teach it to fix that. But if it lists a filename it has never seen, I can't expect it to get it right.
Training on those examples would actually reward hallucinations, which I really don't need more of.
About a third of the sampled sessions produced useful correction examples. I repeated this in three rounds, each time collecting mistakes from the latest model.
Self-correction was one of the more effective training changes. Along with some additional training data, it improved PresetBench (defined below) from 24/47 to 38/47 at int4.
In total, training the model and its later refinements took roughly 75 GPU-hours on an RTX 4090.
Testing

I use three tests. ShellBench has 106 commands across 24 handwritten bash sessions, scored by exact output. PresetBench has 47 scripted cases drawn from failures I hit in the demo. Neither test appears in the training data.

The memory test has 32 worlds. Each writes two random values to two files, then reads them back in separate sessions. A world passes only if both readbacks are exact, giving 64 readbacks overall. The names and values never appear in training.
How much does fine-tuning help?
Model
ShellBench /106
File readbacks /13
Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, prompted
Qwen3-0.6B, prompted
WorldTUI
The biggest difference was memory: WorldTUI got 9/13 readbacks right, compared with 2/13 and 3/13 for the prompted models.

It's still far from a reliable filesystem. It handles familiar commands fairly well, but combining them in new ways can quickly break things. For example, after echo green >> colors, running cat colors often doesn't show the appended line.
Making it fast

For a while I stayed away from autoregressive models altogether. A full redraw is around 3,000 tokens, and generating those one at a time seemed hopeless for something that's supposed to feel like a terminal.

But they just performed so much better than the alternatives I tried, so I gave in. With one token at a time, typing felt fine at ~38 ms per key, but anything that redraws the whole screen (vim test.txt, man, clear) took up to 12 s on my RTX 4090, exactly as feared. Plenty of time to reconsider whether I needed the manual. And I wanted this to run on my Mac, in near real-time.
Rows in parallel

What I'd missed was that most rows in a frame don't depend on each other, so there's no reason to generate them one after another. I run one batch element per row. Each gets the same previous history (including KV cache) but generates only its own update.
That changes the decoding cost from the sum of all rows, up to 3,000 steps, to the length of the longest row, roughly 100 steps.
The cursor then becomes its own step at the end that can see the whole set of row updates.
This required a matching attention mask during training, but the speed improvement was worth it. Large-frame p95 latency dropped from 6.7 s to 0.87 s.
Large-frame p95 latency (RTX 4090) ↓
Rows that can't talk to each other

This might sound too good to be true, and it was.
The issue is that since rows are independent, they can't coordinate, which led to vim opening on row 3 instead of row 0, or several rows adding food for snake at once.
The solution was speculative decoding.
Normally speculative decoding uses a small model to draft tokens and a larger model to verify them. Thanks to causal attention, several tokens can be verified in a single forward pass.
Here I use the same model for both: the parallel rows produce a draft, which the model then verifies sequentially.
The verifier keeps tokens up to the first disagreement. From there it generates its own correction and re-proposes the remaining draft.
In the browser on my M4 Mac, typing a single character takes about 60ms. A larger update like man test takes 2.5s sequentially, or 0.9s with parallel drafting and verification.
Making it smaller

I started with Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, which has roughly 494M parameters. I really wanted a web demo, so I needed to shrink it. The embedding table for its 151,936-token vocabulary is 136M parameters. I only need my 333 tokens, so I can drop almost all of it, which takes the model from 494M to about 360M parameters (990MB → 716MB).
I then quantized it to int4, which brought it to 208 MB.

The browser demo uses a custom JavaScript implementation of the Qwen decoder, with compute shaders written in WGSL and run through WebGPU. The shaders unpack the 4-bit weights during inference. Activations and the attention cache use 32-bit floats. All inference runs locally in the tab.
Distilling

Distilling it into fewer layers taught me something about which layers memory depends on. The teacher was an earlier checkpoint, which scored 78/106 on ShellBench. Removing just layer 7 without retraining barely changed next-token accuracy: 99.3% fell to 98.9%. But exact memory readbacks fell from 64/64 to 0/64. These tests fed in the true history, so the failure wasn't caused by errors compounding on the model's own output.

My first distilled student kept every even-numbered layer, but used the final layer, 23, instead of 22. It still wrote plausible terminal output, but returned the right value in only 31/64 memory readbacks. It always printed one of the two values it had written, but picked the wrong one about half the time. That's chance, and it hadn't recovered after 480M training tokens.

That student had dropped layers 1, 7, 15 and 22. A 16-layer student that kept those four passed all 32 memory test worlds, with 64/64 exact readbacks. It still passed all 32 worlds at 4-bit, at about 138MB. There was a cost elsewhere, though: it got 65 ShellBench commands right against the teacher's 78. So a student can look fine and have quietly lost its memory.
In the end I gave up on distilling it.
What it can do
Memory

This was the part I was most interested in.
Generating a convincing directory listing is easy. What I wanted was to create a file, edit it, wander off, and come back to find it unchanged.
The first time I started tmux, opened a file in vim, changed it, saved it and then in a different tmux window read the updated contents with cat, I felt like Dr. Frankenstein: it's alive!
https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/videos/worldtui-vim-copy.mp4
Other applications
It was very important to me that this should work beyond the bash prompt, so I trained on vim, python, man pages, snake and even tmux.
In vim, it handles the mode switch on esc and lets me save, quit or go back into insert mode.
https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/videos/worldtui-snake.mp4
What really blew my mind was tmux: I can create multiple panes, do various things in each and jump between them. It's not perfect, but it's a small model.
https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/videos/worldtui-tmux.mp4
It even manages environment variables and variable expansion.
https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/videos/worldtui-env.mp4
Python

Since the base model is a coding model, I was curious how it would handle the Python REPL. It makes a decent attempt: small additions are usually right, and list comprehensions return a list, though often with the wrong contents. It's also slightly forgiving of typos: pythoon launches Python, but ython doesn't.
https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/videos/worldtui-python.mp4
What doesn't work

I didn't allow the Docker containers internet access, so tools like lynx are fairly boring.
Python can handle very simple operations, but anything harder produces answers that remind me of GPT-3-era hallucinations.

Sometimes, when I create nested directories, it gets lost and all of a sudden I'm in a different path.
There's clearly a lot of room to improve consistency.
In my testing, the demo ran about 20× slower in Firefox than in Chrome. It uses WebGPU in both. I haven't managed to establish the cause.
As always with projects like this, I tried to solve it myself first and only then looked at how others had approached it.
Back in 2022, people were already prompting ChatGPT to act as a Linux terminal. More recently, GameNGen simulated Doom using diffusion, and NeuralOS tackled a desktop GUI.
WorldTUI is closer to the original ChatGPT terminal trick, except that it's trained specifically on keypresses and screen updates, including full-screen applications like vim and tmux.
Summary
I had a blast building this. Is it useful? Not really. But for a 360M-parameter model running in a browser tab, it's far better than I expected.
What interests me most is that it manages to maintain a somewhat consistent world without implementing any of the rules underneath.

It's obviously a pretty weak world model, and I'd love to see how far this approach could go with better consistency and a different way of generating screen updates, perhaps using diffusion instead of autoregressive decoding.

One experiment I want to try next is training on thousands of randomly generated applications, each with its own controls and rules. The idea is to see whether the model can learn to predict the behaviour of an application it has never encountered before, given enough contextual clues.
Try it here. It's a 208 MB download, runs entirely locally, and works best in Chrome. Try to break it, and let me know what you find.
I'll post the weights soon and add the download link here.

items.title: Code is clay now
items.author: albertodenia
items.summary:
Code is clay now

Alberto Denia ∙ Sep 25, 2026

In the Middle Ages of coding (that is, before November 2025), we coder-stonemasons spent our days meticulously
items.text:
Code is clay now

Alberto Denia ∙ Sep 25, 2026

In the Middle Ages of coding (that is, before November 2025), we coder-stonemasons spent our days meticulously carving code-stone into finished pieces. Stone is unforgiving, and modifying it remained difficult even as better tools improved things over time. Small corrections were okay-ish (some chiseling here, some patching there), but larger ones meant demolition, scaffolding and a careful plan pinned to the wall.

Agentic coding has turned that around: code has become malleable. Even though it’s still made of the same underlying substance as medieval code, the cost of making a change has collapsed. That makes it behave like a different material entirely. Code is clay now.

Working with clay

Once code is clay, you can start modeling it. Slap some big blobs of code-clay into the rough shape you want and see how it feels. Don’t like it? It’s easy to reshape a part or even squash the whole thing and start over. When the overall structure feels right, you refine the way a sculptor does: from the general mass, to the mid-sized features, to the details.

Modeling can be applied fractally, at any layer of the thing you’re building. A solo developer exploring a new product could sketch the entire core in a day to see what works before getting into the details, while a team in charge of a struggling product feature could spend a couple of days taking it in a completely new direction to find out whether the pivot is worth it. No amount of planning or mockups beats watching the actual thing in action.

Your product and engineering judgment still matters, though. Making a change might be nearly free now, but knowing whether it’s the right change isn’t. If you want to build things that feel right and hold together, you can’t just keep piling blobs up. You need to be refining the pieces and thinking about how they fit, or the whole thing will collapse into a sloppity-slop puddle faster than you can prompt your way out of it. Taste, context, guardrails, architecture… those are your armature and your kiln.

When to apply this judgment, and how much of it, is something we are still figuring out. Several workflows are emerging across a spectrum of human involvement. At the extremes of that spectrum sit two approaches worth looking into: artisans and factories.

The way of the artisan

The artisan wants to be in the loop. The fast feedback loop is the best thing about malleable code, and the reason many of us are addicted to it. In the time it takes to get a coffee, you can think of a feature, plan the approach with the agent on your phone and have it ready for review when you come back to your desk. Add some polishing iterations and you have compressed a full product/engineering/QA cycle into one person and thirty minutes.

When you are your own user, the loop gets absurdly satisfying. For example, I’m working on a Markdown editor that I’m using more and more every day. A few days ago I was looking at a file with a list of expenses and I thought: “It’d be cool if I could automatically sum all of them… wait a minute, let me throw some code at it!” Half a soda later, I had the first version of calc blocks (a block that evaluates simple operations and shows the result in its margin) working in the app and already useful. Software development in real time.

Isn’t this just vibe coding? Not necessarily. The way of the artisan is about staying in the loop and applying your judgment to every iteration. When you only judge the user-facing surface, that’s vibe coding. When you also judge the code (its shape at least, if not every line), that’s engineering. The loop is just faster now.

The way of the factory

At the other extreme, you want to remove yourself from the loop. That’s the way of the factory.

The factory is all about building systems that shape code-clay into bricks that fit neatly into a larger structure. Think a pipeline made of specs, generators and verifiers (tests, evals, guardrails, reviewing agents) in loops that only escalate to a human as a last resort. It works best in well-structured codebases with repeatable patterns acting as molds, and clear criteria it can verify its work against. The factory is amazing for things like adding that eleventh CRUD endpoint or grinding through a hundred minor bugs.

Judgment still exists in the factory; it has just moved upstream or been embedded in the pipeline. The jury is still out on how much of it can be embedded and automated, but I suspect setting up the factory so it produces reliable outcomes is a lot of what engineering is about to become.

Artisan or factory?

In both cases, human judgment is still steering the work. The difference lies in when it is applied. The artisan applies it at every iteration, which is great for exploring ideas and refining features that need to feel right. The factory applies it upfront, when building the pipeline, and as little as possible during the loop. Neither can afford to skip it.

You’d think that, given the industrial connotations, factories only belong in large corporate codebases, whereas artisans are indie hackers tinkering with their apps from a beach in Thailand. But the two can be complementary, and many real-life workflows will look like a mix of both. Large, established products need artisanship to solve novel problems or add features that have to feel right. And even solo developers will want to run factories to take care of the boring, repeatable parts, and to achieve a scale that was unthinkable for a single person before. The point is to pick the right approach for the problem you are trying to solve. Which, as it turns out, is what software engineering has always been about.

So we have this new material in our hands. Code is clay now. What will we build with it?

items.title: OpenAI CLI
items.author: armcat
items.summary:
The official CLI for the OpenAI REST API.

brew install openai/tools/openai

To test or install the CLI locally, you need Go version 1.26 or later
items.text:
The official CLI for the OpenAI REST API.

brew install openai/tools/openai

To test or install the CLI locally, you need Go version 1.26 or later installed.

go install 'github.com/openai/openai-cli/cmd/openai@latest'

Once you have run go install, the binary is placed in your Go bin directory:

Default location: $HOME/go/bin (or $GOPATH/bin if GOPATH is set)

Check your path: Run go env GOPATH to see the base directory

If commands aren't found after installation, add the Go bin directory to your PATH:

# Add to your shell profile (.zshrc, .bashrc, etc.)
export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin"

The first eligible interactive openai run quietly saves image picker Tab
shortcuts for future Bash, zsh, and fish sessions. Open a new terminal to use
them. See shortcut setup and removal for
requirements and opt-out. PowerShell keeps normal Tab completion; press Enter
after openai images generate to open the picker.

Bare openai checks for newer stable releases when stdin, stdout, and stderr are terminals.
It adds a plain-text notice below help, at most once every seven days.
Explicit help, commands, completion, CI, and redirected streams skip the check entirely.

The notice includes an update command when the CLI can verify its installation method.
Verified Homebrew installations use brew upgrade --cask openai/tools/openai.
Go commands require a verified binary, an available Go command, and an explicit matching GOBIN.
Custom GOOS or GOARCH settings select the installation guide instead.
Go upgrades to major version 2 or later also select the installation guide.
Unknown installations receive the installation-guide link instead.
The CLI never installs updates automatically.

Checks use public GitHub release metadata without API credentials, at most once daily.
Checks respect HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY, including their lowercase forms.
Update discovery waits at most 200 milliseconds. Failed checks remain silent.
Package-manager availability can lag a new GitHub release.
Set OPENAI_CLI_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to disable checks and notices.

After cloning the git repository for this project, you can use the
scripts/run script to run the tool locally:

The CLI follows a resource-based command structure:

openai <resource> [subresource...] <command> [flags...]

Standard API endpoints require an API key:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
openai responses create \
--input "Say this is a test" \
--model gpt-5.5

Admin endpoints require an admin API key:

export OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY="sk-admin-..."
openai admin organization usage completions \
--start-time 1735689600 \
--end-time 1735776000 \
--bucket-width 1d

Browse each group with --help, for example openai admin --help or
openai admin organization --help. Existing colon commands such as
openai admin:organization:usage completions continue to work.

Run openai to browse command groups by task, with descriptions for each group.
Group help separates actions from nested command groups and lists every immediate command.
Help works without an API key or network connection:

openai help setup # Enter your API key safely
openai images generate --help # Example and every image option
openai help images generate # The same complete image help
openai --help # Command groups and global options

Add --help (or -h) to any command for its complete help page.
openai help COMMAND shows the same page.
Command pages list global options. Use openai --help for their full descriptions.
You can place --help after valid command options.
The old help --all spelling prints migration guidance and the complete page.
Command behavior, defaults, and output formats remain unchanged.
Tab completion follows the same group order and supports help topics and file input paths.
After upgrading, reload shell completion to enable the new file-path behavior.
Older loaded completion scripts keep their previous behavior until refreshed.

Enable command insertion to fill your command line
from examples, setup guidance, and recovery commands. Ctrl+X, then Tab searches suggestions
without running them. Double Tab is an optional binding for Bash, zsh, and fish.

Successful JSON responses print readable text by default, including in pipes.
Use --format json or --format jsonl in scripts that parse API data.
See reading command results for extraction, binary
output, and the scope of readable presentation.

Upload a local file with an explicit purpose, inspect its metadata, then download its contents:

openai files upload "upload space.txt" --purpose user_data
openai files get file-example
openai files download file-example --output "downloaded copy.txt"
openai files download file-example > copy.txt

Replace file-example with the returned file ID. Upload takes a plain path, without an added @.
create, retrieve, content, and their existing flags remain available.
See working with files for literal filenames, output formats, and script examples.

openai images generate --prompt "A tiny orange robot" saves images to
~/Downloads/gpt-images/ and prints their paths, including in pipes. The CLI
uses gpt-image-2.5-sunburst when saving without an explicit model or legacy
response format. Use --model for another exact ID, --name for a filename,
or --output-dir for an existing directory. Existing files are kept.
--format json returns API data without saving or applying the CLI preset.
images edit also saves new results while keeping source files.
images create-variation is retired and no longer available. To create a
variation, use images edit with a GPT Image model and a prompt. See
image generation and saving for commands
and defaults.

openai images preview "path/to/image.png" redisplays a saved image without an
API request. Use openai images inline on or off to remember whether future
saved images appear automatically. Per-command --inline auto, on or off
overrides that setting. on also permits an image font in local Apple Terminal.

Errors print actionable summaries to stderr by default. Use --format-error json
for original API error details, including unknown fields and SDK-reported stream
error events. For those events, extraction paths include the error envelope,
for example --transform-error error.code. Explicit --format
values json, jsonl, raw, and yaml also apply to errors unless overridden
by --format-error; an explicit --format-error auto or text restores summaries.
--transform-error extracts error data independently of successful output.
Malformed or empty error bodies receive a safe diagnostic; HTTP status is included
only when the SDK retains it. Summaries omit rejected values and request URLs;
explicit API error details can contain server-supplied sensitive data.

Environment variable

Required

Default value

OPENAI_API_KEY

no

null

OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY

no

null

OPENAI_ORG_ID

no

null

OPENAI_PROJECT_ID

no

null

OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET

no

null

OPENAI_CUSTOM_HEADERS

no

null

OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_FILE

no

null

OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_KEY_FILE

no

null

OPENAI_UNTRUSTED_STDIN

no

false

--api-key (can also be set with OPENAI_API_KEY env var)

--admin-api-key (can also be set with OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY env var)

--organization (can also be set with OPENAI_ORG_ID env var)

--project (can also be set with OPENAI_PROJECT_ID env var)

--webhook-secret (can also be set with OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET env var)

--mtls-client-cert-file (can also be set with OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_FILE env var)

--mtls-client-key-file (can also be set with OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_KEY_FILE env var)

--help - Show command line usage

--debug - Enable debug logging. This includes HTTP request/response details and bodies; do not share debug logs if they may contain sensitive payloads.

--version, -v - Show the CLI version

--base-url - Use a custom API backend URL. HTTPS is required except for
localhost or literal loopback IP addresses such as 127.0.0.1 and ::1.
This also applies to OPENAI_BASE_URL; remote HTTP backends must enable HTTPS.

--header, -H - Add a literal request header as Name: Value; repeat for multiple headers

--format - Change the output format (auto, text, explore, json, jsonl, pretty, raw, yaml); auto selects readable text unless extracting data

--format-error - Change the stderr error format (auto, text, explore, json, jsonl, pretty, raw, yaml); auto selects readable summaries unless extracting error data

--transform - Transform the data output using GJSON syntax

--transform-error - Transform the error output using GJSON syntax

Use --header or -H before or after a resource command:

openai --header 'X-Trace-ID: example-123' models list \
-H 'X-Client-Label: local,manual'

Values are literal: commas and colons are preserved, and @ prefixes do not
read files. Surrounding spaces and tabs are trimmed from values. -H 'X-Example:'
sends an empty value. If a name is repeated, the last value wins regardless of
case, overriding default and endpoint-specific headers. Headers managed by the
HTTP transport, such as Host and Content-Length, retain the transport's
behavior. Supplied header values are hidden in help and redacted in debug logs.

For credential-bearing headers, have a secret manager or trusted launcher set
OPENAI_CUSTOM_HEADERS directly in the CLI's environment. This keeps credentials
out of command arguments and avoids typing literal secrets into shell history.
The variable accepts one Name: Value entry per line. For example, with
non-sensitive values:

export OPENAI_CUSTOM_HEADERS='X-Trace-ID: example-123
X-Client-Label: local,manual'
openai models list

--header and endpoint-specific header flags override matching environment
entries. Environment header values are also redacted in debug logs. Use
OPENAI_API_KEY and OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY for standard API and admin authentication.

Mutual TLS is currently in beta. To opt in and activate a CA certificate for
your organization or project, follow the
OpenAI Mutual TLS Beta Program
instructions.

To authenticate API-key requests with a mutual TLS client certificate, provide
the client certificate and private key as separate PEM files. If certificate
chain support is enabled for your organization, the certificate file must
contain the leaf certificate first, followed by any intermediate certificates.
Otherwise, use a client certificate signed directly by an activated CA
certificate.

export OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_FILE=/run/secrets/openai/client-chain.pem
export OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/openai/client.key
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://mtls.api.openai.com/v1

Both mTLS files must be configured together. Keep the private key in a
permission-restricted file; do not put private-key contents directly in command

mTLS endpoint, so configure OPENAI_BASE_URL or --base-url explicitly. HTTP
and SOCKS proxies remain supported, but HTTPS proxies are rejected to prevent
presenting the client certificate during the proxy's own TLS handshake.

Passing files as arguments

For JSON input values, @myfile.ext reads local file contents:

Binary upload flags use plain paths. For example, use files upload --file "upload space.txt" --purpose user_data.
Here, --file "@upload space.txt" names an actual file starting with @; it does not expand another file reference.
See working with files.

openai <command> --arg @abe.jpg

Files can also be passed inside JSON or YAML blobs:

openai <command> --arg '{image: "@abe.jpg"}'
# Equivalent:
openai <command> <<YAML
arg:
image: "@abe.jpg"
YAML

escape the @ sign to avoid accidentally passing a file.

base64-encoded string literal (for binary files). If you need to explicitly send

base64-encoding). Note that absolute paths will begin with @file:// or
@data://, followed by a third / (for example, @file:///tmp/file.txt).

items.title: The compiler was supposed to end programming too
items.author: theanonymousone
items.summary:
It’s 7:40 on a Tuesday morning in 2031, and you haven’t written a line of code yet. You probably won’t today, and that’s fine.

While you slept, four agents
items.text:
It’s 7:40 on a Tuesday morning in 2031, and you haven’t written a line of code yet. You probably won’t today, and that’s fine.

While you slept, four agents worked through the backlog you sorted yesterday afternoon. Three of them finished. Their pull requests are waiting for you, each with the tests it added, a short recording of the feature working, and a note about the parts it wasn’t sure of. The fourth agent stopped at 2:13 a.m. and left you a question instead:

The spec says refunds go back to the original card. This customer’s card expired in March. What should happen?

The agent could write refund code all day long. What it can’t do is decide what your company owes a customer whose card has expired, so it stopped and asked, which is exactly what you’d want from a new hire too. Your morning goes like this: you read three pull requests, you go and talk to someone in support, and you write the rule down so clearly that nobody (human or otherwise) has to guess again.

Imagined · Tuesday, 2031

22:0002:0006:0010:0014:0018:0022:00

Agents

122:00 Three agents work through yesterday's backlog and open three pull requests, each with tests and a recording.

222:00 A fourth agent stops and leaves a question: refunds go to the original card, but that card expired.

313:00 Agents build the refund rule you wrote down, with the tests you wrote first.

421:30 Tonight's runs start from the plan you approved.

You

507:40 Read the three pull requests and watch the recordings.

609:00 Answer the 02:13 question. You can't, yet.

710:00 Ask support what customers with expired cards expect.

811:00 Write the rule down as a short spec and five tests.

914:00 Read the agents' work on the one part that touches money.

1016:30 Approve tonight's plan. Go home.

I made that Tuesday up. None of it is science fiction, though. Agents that work unattended overnight exist today, and one of them runs on my own machine every night at ten. It invents a small project, builds it, tests it, and I find out what it made over breakfast. The first morning, I had no idea what it had built. That build is now Rule Safari, a live project on this site, with an article explaining how it works.

So is this the end of programming? People have been asking that for more than seventy years. I find that comforting. I also find it a little suspicious.

Programming has been ending since 1954

On 10 November 1954, IBM’s Programming Research Group finished a preliminary report on a new language called FORTRAN. One sentence in it says that FORTRAN “should virtually eliminate coding and debugging.”

I love this sentence. It’s so sure of itself, and it even came with a budget: problems solved “for less than half the cost” of doing it without FORTRAN. The industry had a name for this kind of thing back then. Assemblers and compilers were called automatic programming. You’d describe what you wanted, and the machine would write the program.

FORTRAN shipped in 1957, and it really did eliminate a kind of coding. Almost nobody translates formulas into machine instructions by hand anymore. Debugging survived just fine. (This month I chased a Scry bug that came down to a bookmark saved only every twelve hours, so I can confirm debugging is alive and well.)

What FORTRAN actually did was take one tedious part of the job away and move the job up a level. People stopped thinking about registers and started thinking about bigger problems. Programs got cheaper to write, so everybody wanted more of them. That has happened over and over since.

Assembly languageYou stopped: writing instructions as raw numbersKathleen Booth, "Coding for A.R.C."

1947

FORTRANYou stopped: translating formulas into machine instructions by handThe 1954 report: it "should virtually eliminate coding and debugging."

1957

CYou stopped: rewriting the same program for every new machine

1972

The Last OneYou stopped: nothing, as it turned outA BASIC program generator, named as the last program you would ever need to buy.

1981

Stack OverflowYou stopped: solving every error message alone

2008

npmYou stopped: writing your own everything

2010

GitHub CopilotYou stopped: typing the boilerplate

2021

Coding agentsYou stopped: typing most of the code

2025

NextYou stopped: ?

20??

My favorite rung is 1981. A British company called D.J. “AI” Systems (yes, really) sold a BASIC program generator named The Last One. The name was the whole pitch. It would write all your programs for you, so it would be the last program you’d ever need to buy.

Reviewers found it useful for some business programs. It was not the last one.

Here’s the pattern on every rung. Something gets automated, the people doing the work stop doing that thing by hand, and the field keeps growing anyway. GitHub counted more than 180 million developers in its 2025 report, and more than 36 million of them had joined in the previous twelve months.

So I don’t think AI ends programming. I do think this rung is different in one way, and that’s speed. GitHub Copilot’s preview came out in June 2021. By 2025, 84% of developers in Stack Overflow’s survey were using AI tools or planning to. Four years, from novelty to default.

What 2026 actually looks like

The vibes are loud right now, so let’s start with numbers. (Speaking of vibes: Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” in February 2025, for the kind of coding where you “fully give in to the vibes.” Stack Overflow asked about it that year. 72% of developers said it isn’t part of their professional work, and another 5% said emphatically no. I love that they offered that option.)

Stack Overflow’s survey is the biggest regular check-up we have, and the adoption curve in it is steep: from 70% of developers using AI tools or planning to in 2023, to 84% in 2025, when half of professional developers were using them every day.

You’d think all that use would mean developers love these tools. Nope. Favorable sentiment fell from 77% in 2023 to 60% in 2025, and only ticked back up to 62% this year. In 2025, more developers distrusted the accuracy of AI output (46%) than trusted it (33%). The top frustration, picked by 66% of them, was “AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite.”

I feel seen. Almost right is an expensive kind of wrong, because you have to read every line to find the part that isn’t. (45% of them said debugging AI-generated code takes longer.)

20%40%60%80%100%202320242025202670%76%84%use or plan to77%72%60%62%favorable42%43%33%trust accuracy

Then there’s my favorite study of the whole AI boom, mostly because it’s so rude. In early 2025, METR, a nonprofit research group, ran a proper randomized controlled trial. Sixteen experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real issues in their own repositories, projects they’d been on for years, and each issue was randomly assigned to allow AI tools or ban them.

Before they started, the developers expected AI to cut their time by 24%. When they finished, they believed it had cut it by 20%. The clock said that with AI they took 19% longer.

Nineteen percent longer! And they walked away sure it had helped.

← longershorter →

Economists predictedexpert forecast39% less time

ML researchers predictedexpert forecast38% less time

The developers expectedbefore the tasks24% less time

The developers feltafter the tasks20% less time

The clock measuredwhat happened19% more time

Before anyone screenshots that for a hot take: it’s one study of sixteen people, using early-2025 tools, on codebases they knew better than any model could.

And METR tried to run it again. A bigger study started in August 2025, with 57 developers and more than 800 tasks, and in February 2026 METR said the data was too unreliable to lean on. Mostly that was because developers kept declining to take part, since they “do not wish to work without AI.” The early numbers hinted at an 18% speedup for the returning developers (with a range wide enough to include no speedup at all).

I think that’s the most 2026 way an experiment has ever failed. People refused to be in the group without AI.

What I take from METR is narrower than any headline, and more useful: how fast you feel is not a measurement. If you want to know whether AI makes your team faster, measure it the way you’d measure anything else.

The line that keeps going up

METR’s other big project tracks how long a task an AI agent can finish on its own. They time human experts on a suite of software tasks, then find the task length where an agent succeeds half the time. In 2019, GPT-2 managed tasks that take a person about three seconds. GPT-4 got to about four minutes in 2023. Claude 3.7 Sonnet reached an hour in February 2025, and Claude Opus 4.6 reached about twelve hours a year later.

Across the whole series, that number has doubled about every six months. Since 2023, it’s been closer to every four months.

1 min1 hour1 workday1 work week1 work month2019202120232025202720292031if the trend holdsGPT-2GPT-4Claude 3.7 SonnetGPT-5Claude Opus 4.6

Now, a log-scale chart with a dashed line on the end is how a lot of bad predictions start, so let me be careful. “Half the time” is doing a lot of work in that definition. Benchmark tasks are cleaner than your codebase. And METR stopped updating that page in September. But if the line keeps going even roughly, agents will handle a month of human work, half the time, around 2028. That’s where my 2031 Tuesday comes from. I didn’t pull it out of thin air. I pulled it out of a log-scale chart, which is thin air with axes.

The companies building these things are already living a version of it. Google said in October 2024 that more than a quarter of its new code was generated by AI, and “well over 30%” six months later. In March 2025, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei predicted AI would be writing 90% of code within three to six months. That was too soon. But by May 2026, Anthropic said more than 80% of the code merged into its own codebase was written by Claude.

When code gets cheap, the queue moves

Make one step of a process faster and the work piles up in front of the next slowest step. Anyone who has worked a kitchen on a Saturday night knows this: speed up the grill and the plates start waiting at the pass.

That’s what’s happening to software teams. In 2025, Faros AI looked at telemetry from more than 10,000 developers on 1,255 teams. Developers on teams with high AI adoption finished 21% more tasks and merged 98% more pull requests, and their review time went up 91%.

Faros ran it again in 2026 with 22,000 developers. Task completion per developer was up 34%, which sounds great until you read the rest. Median review time had grown five times. 31% more pull requests were merging without any review at all, and the ratio of incidents to pull requests had more than tripled.

The code got cheaper, the reading got more expensive, and some teams quietly stopped reading. That matters because the code isn’t always good. Veracode tested more than 100 language models on 80 coding tasks in 2025, and 45% of the results had a security flaw. GitClear found that copy-pasted lines went from 8.3% of changed code in 2021 to 12.3% in 2024, while moved code, the kind you get from refactoring, fell from about a quarter to under 10%.

Spare a thought for the maintainers, too. Daniel Stenberg, who leads curl, started banning people who submitted “AI slop” bug reports in May 2025, writing that the project was “effectively being DDoSed.” In January 2026, curl shut down its bug bounty.

201920262031, a guess

Decide what to build

Write it down

Write the code

Review it

Check it works

Ship and run it

Today: code arrives faster than people can read it, so pull requests wait for review.

Fred Brooks saw a version of this coming in 1986. In “No Silver Bullet” he split the difficulties of software into two piles, borrowing Aristotle’s words: essence and accidents. The accidents are the trouble our tools cause us, like syntax, boilerplate and fighting the build. The essence is what he called “the specification, design, and testing of this conceptual construct,” which is a fancy way of saying: working out what the thing should do. AI is getting very good at the accidents. The essence is the refund question from 2:13 a.m., and it’s still on your desk.

The rung we might be sawing off

This is the part of the data I like least.

In August 2025, Erik Brynjolfsson and two colleagues at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab used ADP payroll data to look at who was getting hired. Employment for software developers aged 22 to 25 was down nearly 20% from its peak in late 2022. Older developers showed no noticeable change.

They updated the study this August, with data through June 2026. Young workers in AI-exposed jobs are now 19% below where they’d be if they had kept pace with less-exposed peers. Experienced workers show no comparable gap. Most of the effect comes from companies hiring fewer young people in the first place.

The rest of the market isn’t exactly roaring either. Indeed’s index of software development job postings sits about 21% below February 2020, after bottoming out 39% below in May 2025.

The Stanford authors are careful to call their findings descriptive, not causal, and plenty else has happened since 2022. Interest rates went up, and a lot of companies had hired too many people during the pandemic (Indeed’s index peaked at more than twice its 2020 level in early 2022). But the pattern lines up uncomfortably well with what agents are good at: the small, well-defined ticket we used to give the new person on the team.

Senior engineers get made on the job, mostly by being juniors on real teams: doing the boring tickets, breaking production once, and having someone kind explain why. My guess is that the teams doing well in 2035 will be the ones that kept hiring juniors in 2026 and gave them a different apprenticeship: reviewing agent work with a senior beside them, owning one small system end to end, and writing the specs and tests the agents build from. Writing those specs and tests is a real job. It might turn out to be the job.

Five guesses for 2031

Okay, now the guessing part. Bookmark this page and come back in 2031 to laugh at me.

Teams get smaller, and there are a lot more of them. According to Y Combinator’s Jared Friedman, a quarter of the Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were about 95% AI-generated. (Yes, that’s the 1954 promise again. Maybe this time it sticks.)

I expect that to change, with something like “verification engineer” on job boards and much better tooling that shows a reviewer the recording, the risky lines and the tests the agent didn’t write. The Faros numbers say we need it now, never mind in 2031.

Every change carries a label. I think a pull request will routinely say who or what wrote it, who checked it, and what was actually verified. I already do a small version of this: every project my nightly agent builds says so, in its README and on this site.

Back to Tuesday

FORTRAN did eliminate a kind of coding. It didn’t eliminate coders. It made a lot more of them, working on harder problems, and the debugging came along for the ride.

I think AI does the same thing, faster and messier. The developer of 2031 spends the day deciding what should exist, explaining it clearly enough that a machine can build it, and checking that what came back is right. That was always the hard part. We just had less time for it because we were busy typing.

What does your Tuesday look like right now? Are you reviewing more than you write? Tell me in the comments. I’d like to know if my guess is already wrong.

blocks.x: It’s 7:40 on a Tuesday morning in 2031, and you haven’t written a line of code yet. You probably won’t today, and that’s fine.

While you slept, four agents worked through the backlog you sorted yesterday afternoon. Three of them finished. Their pull requests are waiting for you, each with the tests it added, a short recording of the feature working, and a note about the parts it wasn’t sure of. The fourth agent stopped at 2:13 a.m. and left you a question instead:
The spec says refunds go back to the original card. This customer’s card expired in March. What should happen?

The agent could write refund code all day long. What it can’t do is decide what your company owes a customer whose card has expired, so it stopped and asked, which is exactly what you’d want from a new hire too. Your morning goes like this: you read three pull requests, you go and talk to someone in support, and you write the rule down so clearly that nobody (human or otherwise) has to guess again.
Imagined · Tuesday, 2031
Agents

222:00 A fourth agent stops and leaves a question: refunds go to the original card, but that card expired.
313:00 Agents build the refund rule you wrote down, with the tests you wrote first.
421:30 Tonight's runs start from the plan you approved.

507:40 Read the three pull requests and watch the recordings.
609:00 Answer the 02:13 question. You can't, yet.

811:00 Write the rule down as a short spec and five tests.
914:00 Read the agents' work on the one part that touches money.

I made that Tuesday up. None of it is science fiction, though. Agents that work unattended overnight exist today, and one of them runs on my own machine every night at ten. It invents a small project, builds it, tests it, and I find out what it made over breakfast. The first morning, I had no idea what it had built. That build is now Rule Safari, a live project on this site, with an article explaining how it works.
So is this the end of programming? People have been asking that for more than seventy years. I find that comforting. I also find it a little suspicious.
Programming has been ending since 1954

On 10 November 1954, IBM’s Programming Research Group finished a preliminary report on a new language called FORTRAN. One sentence in it says that FORTRAN “should virtually eliminate coding and debugging.”

I love this sentence. It’s so sure of itself, and it even came with a budget: problems solved “for less than half the cost” of doing it without FORTRAN. The industry had a name for this kind of thing back then. Assemblers and compilers were called automatic programming. You’d describe what you wanted, and the machine would write the program.

FORTRAN shipped in 1957, and it really did eliminate a kind of coding. Almost nobody translates formulas into machine instructions by hand anymore. Debugging survived just fine. (This month I chased a Scry bug that came down to a bookmark saved only every twelve hours, so I can confirm debugging is alive and well.)

What FORTRAN actually did was take one tedious part of the job away and move the job up a level. People stopped thinking about registers and started thinking about bigger problems. Programs got cheaper to write, so everybody wanted more of them. That has happened over and over since.
Assembly languageYou stopped: writing instructions as raw numbersKathleen Booth, "Coding for A.R.C."
FORTRANYou stopped: translating formulas into machine instructions by handThe 1954 report: it "should virtually eliminate coding and debugging."
CYou stopped: rewriting the same program for every new machine
The Last OneYou stopped: nothing, as it turned outA BASIC program generator, named as the last program you would ever need to buy.
Stack OverflowYou stopped: solving every error message alone
npmYou stopped: writing your own everything
GitHub CopilotYou stopped: typing the boilerplate
Coding agentsYou stopped: typing most of the code
NextYou stopped: ?

My favorite rung is 1981. A British company called D.J. “AI” Systems (yes, really) sold a BASIC program generator named The Last One. The name was the whole pitch. It would write all your programs for you, so it would be the last program you’d ever need to buy.
Reviewers found it useful for some business programs. It was not the last one.

Here’s the pattern on every rung. Something gets automated, the people doing the work stop doing that thing by hand, and the field keeps growing anyway. GitHub counted more than 180 million developers in its 2025 report, and more than 36 million of them had joined in the previous twelve months.

So I don’t think AI ends programming. I do think this rung is different in one way, and that’s speed. GitHub Copilot’s preview came out in June 2021. By 2025, 84% of developers in Stack Overflow’s survey were using AI tools or planning to. Four years, from novelty to default.
What 2026 actually looks like

The vibes are loud right now, so let’s start with numbers. (Speaking of vibes: Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” in February 2025, for the kind of coding where you “fully give in to the vibes.” Stack Overflow asked about it that year. 72% of developers said it isn’t part of their professional work, and another 5% said emphatically no. I love that they offered that option.)

Stack Overflow’s survey is the biggest regular check-up we have, and the adoption curve in it is steep: from 70% of developers using AI tools or planning to in 2023, to 84% in 2025, when half of professional developers were using them every day.

You’d think all that use would mean developers love these tools. Nope. Favorable sentiment fell from 77% in 2023 to 60% in 2025, and only ticked back up to 62% this year. In 2025, more developers distrusted the accuracy of AI output (46%) than trusted it (33%). The top frustration, picked by 66% of them, was “AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite.”
I feel seen. Almost right is an expensive kind of wrong, because you have to read every line to find the part that isn’t. (45% of them said debugging AI-generated code takes longer.)

Then there’s my favorite study of the whole AI boom, mostly because it’s so rude. In early 2025, METR, a nonprofit research group, ran a proper randomized controlled trial. Sixteen experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real issues in their own repositories, projects they’d been on for years, and each issue was randomly assigned to allow AI tools or ban them.
Before they started, the developers expected AI to cut their time by 24%. When they finished, they believed it had cut it by 20%. The clock said that with AI they took 19% longer.
Nineteen percent longer! And they walked away sure it had helped.
← longershorter →
Economists predictedexpert forecast39% less time
ML researchers predictedexpert forecast38% less time
The developers expectedbefore the tasks24% less time
The developers feltafter the tasks20% less time
The clock measuredwhat happened19% more time
Before anyone screenshots that for a hot take: it’s one study of sixteen people, using early-2025 tools, on codebases they knew better than any model could.

And METR tried to run it again. A bigger study started in August 2025, with 57 developers and more than 800 tasks, and in February 2026 METR said the data was too unreliable to lean on. Mostly that was because developers kept declining to take part, since they “do not wish to work without AI.” The early numbers hinted at an 18% speedup for the returning developers (with a range wide enough to include no speedup at all).
I think that’s the most 2026 way an experiment has ever failed. People refused to be in the group without AI.

What I take from METR is narrower than any headline, and more useful: how fast you feel is not a measurement. If you want to know whether AI makes your team faster, measure it the way you’d measure anything else.
The line that keeps going up

METR’s other big project tracks how long a task an AI agent can finish on its own. They time human experts on a suite of software tasks, then find the task length where an agent succeeds half the time. In 2019, GPT-2 managed tasks that take a person about three seconds. GPT-4 got to about four minutes in 2023. Claude 3.7 Sonnet reached an hour in February 2025, and Claude Opus 4.6 reached about twelve hours a year later.
Across the whole series, that number has doubled about every six months. Since 2023, it’s been closer to every four months.
1 min1 hour1 workday1 work week1 work month2019202120232025202720292031if the trend holdsGPT-2GPT-4Claude 3.7 SonnetGPT-5Claude Opus 4.6

Now, a log-scale chart with a dashed line on the end is how a lot of bad predictions start, so let me be careful. “Half the time” is doing a lot of work in that definition. Benchmark tasks are cleaner than your codebase. And METR stopped updating that page in September. But if the line keeps going even roughly, agents will handle a month of human work, half the time, around 2028. That’s where my 2031 Tuesday comes from. I didn’t pull it out of thin air. I pulled it out of a log-scale chart, which is thin air with axes.

The companies building these things are already living a version of it. Google said in October 2024 that more than a quarter of its new code was generated by AI, and “well over 30%” six months later. But by May 2026, Anthropic said more than 80% of the code merged into its own codebase was written by Claude.
When code gets cheap, the queue moves

Make one step of a process faster and the work piles up in front of the next slowest step. Anyone who has worked a kitchen on a Saturday night knows this: speed up the grill and the plates start waiting at the pass.

That’s what’s happening to software teams. In 2025, Faros AI looked at telemetry from more than 10,000 developers on 1,255 teams. Developers on teams with high AI adoption finished 21% more tasks and merged 98% more pull requests, and their review time went up 91%.

Faros ran it again in 2026 with 22,000 developers. Task completion per developer was up 34%, which sounds great until you read the rest. Median review time had grown five times. 31% more pull requests were merging without any review at all, and the ratio of incidents to pull requests had more than tripled.

The code got cheaper, the reading got more expensive, and some teams quietly stopped reading. That matters because the code isn’t always good. Veracode tested more than 100 language models on 80 coding tasks in 2025, and 45% of the results had a security flaw. GitClear found that copy-pasted lines went from 8.3% of changed code in 2021 to 12.3% in 2024, while moved code, the kind you get from refactoring, fell from about a quarter to under 10%.

Spare a thought for the maintainers, too. Daniel Stenberg, who leads curl, started banning people who submitted “AI slop” bug reports in May 2025, writing that the project was “effectively being DDoSed.” In January 2026, curl shut down its bug bounty.
Decide what to build
Write it down
Write the code
Review it
Check it works
Ship and run it
Today: code arrives faster than people can read it, so pull requests wait for review.

Fred Brooks saw a version of this coming in 1986. In “No Silver Bullet” he split the difficulties of software into two piles, borrowing Aristotle’s words: essence and accidents. The accidents are the trouble our tools cause us, like syntax, boilerplate and fighting the build. The essence is what he called “the specification, design, and testing of this conceptual construct,” which is a fancy way of saying: working out what the thing should do. AI is getting very good at the accidents. The essence is the refund question from 2:13 a.m., and it’s still on your desk.
